newsitem.title: USA: Florida court strikes down tax-limiting amendments.
newsitem.headline: Florida court strikes down tax-limiting amendments.

text.p: The Florida Supreme Court Thursday struck down a trio of tax-limiting initiatives, ruling that the proposed constitutional amendments were too sweeping.

One amendment would have required voter approval for new taxes. The second would require local and state governments to compensate homeowners if a government action decreased the value of their property.
The third was a technical amendment needed to make the compensation proposal legal. It would have allowed that proposal to address more than one topic.
Florida law allows citizens to initiate constitutional amendments by collecting certified petition signatures from at least 429,000 voters.
The state supreme court must must approve the ballot language to ensure that the title and summary are not misleading and that the amendment address only a single issue.
In an unsigned, unanimous opinion, the court rejected each of the proposals, saying they failed on both counts.
The proposals were sponsored by the Tax Cap Committee, a statewide anti-tax group funded heavily by the sugar industry, and would have been put to voters in November 1998.
Backers said the measures would bring more accountability to government officials by restricting their ability to tax.
Opponents, a coalition including municipal governments, environmentalists and city planners, said the amendments would create financial gridlock.
Tax Cap president David Biddulph declined comment immediately after the ruling, but said the group would issue a statement later Thursday.
It was the second time the court has rejected a Tax Cap proposal requiring voter approval for taxes. In 1994, the court struck down a similar proposal a month before the general election.
The group reworded the proposal, collected new signatures and returned to the court in December to plead its case.
